name: Tetracosactide
lead: Tetracosactide, also known as cosyntropin or ACTH 1-24, is a synthetic peptide made of the first 24 amino acids of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). It prompts the adrenal glands to release cortisol and is mainly used in the ACTH stimulation test, which checks whether the adrenal glands are working.[1][2]

The link to looks is indirect: cortisol balance affects energy, weight, and body composition, and the test helps identify adrenal insufficiency, whose symptoms include fatigue, appetite loss and weight loss, as well as other adrenal and pituitary conditions that change appearance.[3][4] Recovery-oriented communities discuss it in the context of adrenal axis health after steroid or other hormone use.
Brand names include Synacthen and Cortrosyn.[1] In the US the synthetic form is labeled for diagnostic use.

chain: Injected 1-24 ACTH stimulates adrenal cortisol release

angle.text: Tetracosactide is used to test adrenal function. People relate it to appearance through the effects cortisol status has on energy, weight and body composition once a deficiency is found and treated.

quick.overview:
Tetracosactide is a lab-made version of the first 24 amino acids of ACTH, the pituitary hormone that signals the adrenals to make cortisol. It is mostly used as a diagnostic injection.

By showing whether the adrenal glands respond, it helps identify adrenal insufficiency, a cause of fatigue and weight loss that people link to how they look and feel.
quick.mechanism: It binds ACTH receptors on the adrenal cortex and triggers cortisol release. A healthy adrenal gland raises blood cortisol within about 30 minutes of injection, which lets clinicians separate adrenal from pituitary causes of deficiency.[1]
quick.risks: Therapeutic ACTH products can raise infection risk, suppress the HPA axis and cause Cushing-like effects; hypersensitivity is a contraindication.[1] It is a prescription medicine; in the UK it has also been used short-term when glucocorticoids are unsuitable.

paras: The cosyntropin stimulation test is used to diagnose primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency, including glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency, and to confirm non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia.[1][3][5] It is also used as an alternative to the insulin tolerance test in corticotroph deficiency, although its sensitivity is not optimal for partial deficits.[6]
It retains the full activity of ACTH, prompting adrenal glucocorticoid production.[1]
Increased infection risk, HPA-axis suppression and Cushing's syndrome are listed risks for ACTH medications, and contraindications vary by country.[1]

Synthetic ACTH was developed to replace animal-derived corticotropin. Cortrosyn was approved by the FDA in 1970, and UK Synacthen formulations in 2008.[1] ACTH products have also drawn attention for steep price rises and for reports of misuse in professional cycling.[1]

Human studies cover diagnostic testing of adrenal function in adrenal insufficiency, cirrhosis and critical illness, and a randomized trial of cosyntropin for infantile spasms.[3][7][8] None examine appearance outcomes.
